01 — Overview

D.R.E.A.M.S. is a fully autonomous unmanned surface vehicle developed to collect environmental data in degraded aquatic ecosystems. The project was conceived, designed, fabricated, and water-tested within a single semester as a two-person first-year engineering project at Northeastern University's London Scholar Program.

The mission profile targets monitoring of environmentally sensitive water bodies — including the Dead Sea and Bay Area marshlands — where manual data collection is impractical or hazardous. The vessel autonomously navigates to waypoints, collects multi-parameter water quality data via a deployable sensor pod, and transmits results in real time to a shore-side operator.

Every component — from the 3D-printed motor housings and structural reinforcement plates to the sensor pod enclosure and propulsion mounts — was designed in CAD and fabricated in-house using the program's makerspace. The entire system was built and tested within a £100 budget.

02 — Technical Breakdown

Systems & Engineering

Hull & Structure

Catamaran twin-hull configuration selected for superior transverse stability and expanded sensor deck area — consistent with USV research literature. The bridge connecting the two hulls experienced structural flexing under load, resolved through custom-fabricated reinforcement plates designed and iterated in SolidWorks.

  • Acrylic and 3D-printed structural members
  • Custom motor housings for spray protection
  • Hull panels painted and sealed for waterproofing
Propulsion

Differential thrust via two independent motors — one per hull — enabling steering without a rudder. A waterjet system was initially attempted but abandoned after encoder failure and pressure sensor costs exceeded budget. Full root-cause analysis was performed before pivoting to the current solution.

  • Dual independent brushless motors
  • Custom 3D-printed propeller mounts
  • Differential thrust steering logic
Electronics & Computing

Three Raspberry Pi Pico microcontrollers manage the full system — one dedicated to vessel-side operations, one running the sensor payload pod, and one on the shore side for operator communication and control. Shore-side and vessel-side Picos exchange operational data and control commands wirelessly at a verified range of 1,000 meters.

  • 3× Raspberry Pi Pico MCUs (vessel, sensor pod, shore)
  • Long-range wireless communication module
  • Onboard data logging to structured file
  • Excel-importable CSV output format
Sensor Suite

A custom waterproof sensor pod was designed and fabricated to deploy instruments at variable depths below the waterline. An onboard BME280 simultaneously captures atmospheric data above the surface.

  • Temperature, pH, salinity, turbidity, conductivity
  • BME280: atmospheric temp, humidity, pressure
  • Variable-depth deployment mechanism
  • GPS-tagged timestamped data logging
03 — Safety Architecture

Fault-Tolerant Systems

One of the most technically ambitious aspects of the project was designing a comprehensive multi-layer safety system — engineering typically seen in professional maritime platforms, not first-year student projects.

💧
Water Ingress Detection
Open circuit sensor triggers alert if water enters the hull, enabling early detection before critical damage occurs.
🌡
Motor Thermistors
Thermistors positioned at each motor continuously monitor heat levels and flag overtemperature conditions.
🔋
Battery Monitoring
Real-time battery percentage tracking with progressive low-power warnings transmitted to shore side.
📡
Loss-of-Signal Auto-Return
If communication with shore is lost beyond a set time threshold, the vessel autonomously returns to its launch point.
🆘
SOS Signal
Critical fault conditions trigger an SOS transmission to the shore-side operator for immediate intervention.
⚙️
Fault-Tolerant Mission Continue
Non-critical system failures are reported to shore but do not abort the mission — the vessel continues autonomously.

Additionally: manual override via handheld controller and physical safety tether were used during all water testing.

05 — Outcome

Results & Next Steps

The vessel was successfully water-tested at St Katharine Docks, London — a marina adjacent to campus — following a formal access request process negotiated directly with dock management. The autonomous navigation, wireless communication, and sensor systems all performed as designed during field testing.

The project demonstrated that a capable, multi-system autonomous marine platform can be engineered and deployed by a two-person first-year team within a single semester, on a constrained budget, using only makerspace resources.

Future Development
The team is in discussions with the Port of Oakland to deploy DREAMS for large-scale water quality monitoring and environmental surveillance. This would expand the platform from a student prototype to a real-world environmental monitoring tool used by port operations staff.
